utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Momir Talic and Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I'm sorry we are starting a little bit late. But I had my first mishap -- mishap on the road today. So that's why I'm late. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, good afternoon to you, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian and Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good AFTERNOON to you. Appearance for Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Milka Maglov. I am counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Main counsel John Ackerman and legal assistant Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, and I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Are you alone today?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am all alone today. And before starting -- before starting, I would like to inform the Chamber -- I would like to inform about the interpretation problems that have occurred yesterday. And I realised that -- by reading the transcript yesterday that the errors that occurred were not minor and I really believe that they deeply affected my cross-examination. The question I am referring to is a vital question, the most important question of my entire cross-examination. I asked it 3 times. Three times it contained the words “the first time” and three times these same words were not translated. I would ask to go into private session so that I can explain myself properly and as I am referring to the cross-examination that was in closed session,I prefer to do this in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private or closed?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that private session would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to start again, Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to respond about the what Mr. Ackerman made yesterday about his offered stipulation. That stipulation is very narrow and limited. And I'd like to read just part of it to this Chamber. The stipulation states, in relation to the information yesterday "we do not admit that the killings were done by Bosnian Serb force -- I think that means forces -- or that the persons killed were non-combatants. We only admit that the alleged killings in fact occurred." So obviously those two issues, the status of the persons committing the crime and the status of the victims is something that need to be brought out. I think they're important to the Chamber. They go to the elements of some of these offences. And there would have been no way to go through those incidents without describing the setting and the scene and what he saw, as the witness did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, obviously, but I take Mr. Nicholls's word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I would bring them to you. And I do so now. I believe the document is, you know -- is what it says it is. In every instance in the indictment, the Prosecutor contends that -- that these killings were done by Serb forces. And that is a term that is -- that is very broad and inaccurate and does not serve to impose any particular criminal liability on anyone, as far as I understand it. And therefore, that's why I said that we're not admitting that these things were done by Serb forces. They could very easily have been done by roving bands of camouflage-clad criminals. And I think in many cases they in fact were. I think in fact in the very case we're dealing with right now they were. But in terms of the actual killing that took place, I have admitted every one of them that's in the indictment, with the exception of those that are listed in that letter. And I think it's not necessary to go into the details of the killings and put the witnesses through that part of it. I think the simple question that could be asked is -- I mean, it's very clear in this particular case that there's no question. But what the people involved were non-combatants. But in some of the incidents, it's not quite that clear. So I think it serves to accomplish what I intended to accomplish with it. And if it doesn't, I will certainly consider making some changes. But I can't admit that these things were all done by Serb forces, because I don't think they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But there is a multiplicity of factors here. One, you are also not admitting across the board that the persons killed were non-combatants. And this is with reference to paragraph 38 of the corrected version of the last indictment -- the last corrected version, where there is a number of killings, as you know. And in each and every case, you're not accepting that the persons killed were non-combatants. You're not accepting that the killings were done by Bosnian Serb forces. So basically what you're saying is bring the witness, just the same. Don't tell him -- don't ask the witness to explain how the murder took place, to avoid the trauma. And go straight to simple questions. One is: Do you know who committed -- who did the killing? And secondly: Was or were the persons killed combatants or non-combatants? And I think that's the most unfair way to treat someone who's gone through God knows what, bringing him here, and giving him the impression that we are ignoring all the rest and paying attention only to two simple things: Who did it and who was killed. I mean, he or she would go out of this courtroom saying, "They brought me all the way from wherever to tell the whole story of how my family was exterminated, and they never asked me a question about it." I would suppose -- I mean, I am not going to go any further today. But I am sure, Mr. Ackerman, you've lived enough trials in your life to -- you're experienced enough to know what the victim or the victim's family expect from a trial, which they don't always get because sometimes they -- things are not exactly as they pretend. But -- yes, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the way you have put it is a -- is an entirely different issue. And if in fact it is of some value, cathartically or whatever to this person to actually describe the incident in open court, then I wouldn't want to stand in the way of that. But if it is traumatic and painful for the person to do that, I doubt that they are going to complain that we didn't put them through that trauma and pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not after --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I would certainly be willing to leave it up to the witness whether they want to go through that or not. All I'm trying to do is put the witnesses in a position where if it's too painful and traumatic for them to describe what happened -- and I'm trying to create a situation where they don't have to. That's all I'm trying to do. There's no lawyer tricks involved there. There's no strategy involve there or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is attributing you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not attributing to you any lawyer's trick or so anything of the sort. That's not what we meant. However, let's leave it at this. This is the position that you take and we'll have to act accordingly. Can we bring the witness in now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But we would need to go back into private session and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have some of the blinds brought down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session. And put some of the blinds down, please. And of course everyone is requested to observe the use of pseudonym plus distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I have a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to put them all down?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All down?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was reminded by the Registrar the other day, way back when I was cross-examining Dr. Donia I had said I would be willing to put a copy of the Berg and Shoup book into evidence as an exhibit. And I had heard the Chamber say, "No, you don't need to do that," when I had offered to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't like that. It was -- in a way, we were pulling your leg, Mr. Ackerman. And in another way, we were being very serious in case you meant it different. At the time, you suggested giving a -- making available a copy to each and every one of us three up here. And I said, "No, thank you. We don't need a copy each. If you want to provide the Chamber with a copy, you can do that, but not us." This is in case you were sort of -- but it was said to you in a light manner which we thought you had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I did. But now my question is: Do you -- should I put it on the record or not? I'm perfectly happy to the that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. But it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are handing these books to the Tribunal and not to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will, of course, make good use of that, just as we make good use of your book sometimes. Can we bring the witness in now? Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry, Your Honour, again if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Mr. Nicholls. Now, let -- usher, let me explain to you how to go about it. You are going to read that -- you are going -- you are going to read that statement in English. It will be translated to the witness in B/C/S. He will answer in B/C/S -- he will repeat the same words in B/C/S. And that will be in -- translated into English to us. The problem is he's got a problem which we have to solve that way. So we are going to go about it like -- sir, could you look at me, please. We are going to do exactly like we did yesterday. The statement -- the solemn declaration to tell the truth is going to be read out to you, translated to you. You repeat it like yesterday. And then you can sit down and we can start again. Madam Registrar, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I speak the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. Now, Mr. Nicholls is going -- Mr. Nicholls is going to continue with his examination-in-chief. Now, Mr. Nicholls, if there is anything that you think -- use your best judgement now. If there is anything that you think we needn't ask necessarily details about from the witness, you may tell me exactly what you mean, which part of his statement, for example, and I can deal with it myself as a Chamber. And that will facilitate things and the -- short of objections from the Defence we can bypass any traumas that -- you have to tell me, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you prefer it that way. If you prefer to put questions, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, then, I may lead a little bit through some of the areas which I don't believe are contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move ahead a little bit. Were you given any notices -- did you receive any notices to attend later court hearings in that case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you attend that later court hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't dare attend it. I didn't want to go. I had to prepare myself, to prepare documents, and to prepare to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But just -- when you say you didn't dare to go, is that because, just to be clear, you were afraid to go? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've gone into my -- I think the last area we need to cover. You said you were preparing to leave. Can you briefly describe to the Trial Chamber what you needed to do in order to be able to leave Banja Luka, the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to get all the documents from the municipality, from the company, from the post office that I had no debts. I had to sign also documents that I'd give away everything and that I have no demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in obtaining these documents, were you required to pay any fees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everywhere, everywhere. You could not do anything without money, even in my company. When I get -- to get a certificate, I had to pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after -- were you able to obtain all this documentation that you needed in order to be able to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was helped by some policemen I had to pay in order to get somewhere, because there were so many people. There was a real crowd. So that I could -- so that I would be able to pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did you come to physically leave Banja Luka and leave the country? Was it by foot, by car, by bus, by plane? How were you able to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were three convoys, three buses. And there was this main -- major -- or I don't know, actually, what his rank was. And he had a car. And he was head of the buses. But first of all, we had to pay. These hospitals. I had to pay 950 Deutschmarks. That's what I had to pay to get on the bus for the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the two of us was you and your younger son.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what was the ethnicity of the other people who were on this bus convoy with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there was a Serb who didn't want to go to their army. But I didn't really notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What of your property were you able to bring with you when you finally left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just my clothes, what I had on me. The clothes I wore, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have you heard what became of your home and your farm? Do you know what happened to it, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when I lived over there in the town, there were some neighbours who came and told me, "There, your house is burning." And so everything was destroyed, everything that's -- was round the house as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you hear whether any of the other homes in your small hamlet were destroyed, or was it just your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything. All the hamlets that were Muslim. Everything was destroyed. Nothing was left. Nothing was remained standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Specifically in your hamlet, in the hamlet that was your home from when you were born until --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in other hamlets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So just to be clear- I'm sorry- are you saying that all of the homes in your hamlet were burned down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the Serb family-owned homes in that hamlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Normal. People went on living.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you ever hear whether there was any investigation to try to determine who had burned your home down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau, I suppose you have a few questions. So let me explain to the witness a little bit what's going to happen so that I make things easy for him. Now, sir, the Prosecution has finished with the series of questions it wanted to put to you. The Defence team for the two accused have a right to cross-examine you, to put questions to you as well. The first team is choosing not to put any questions to you, the team for Mr. Brdjanin. You are going to be asked a few questions by the Defence team for General Talic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before I start the cross-examination, I would like to express my sympathy for the tragedy that has occurred to you, and I do apologise in advance for the questions that I am forced to ask you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the way you were dismissed. You said that all the Muslims and all the Croats who did not join the Serb army were dismissed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did certain Muslims and certain Croats did join the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did these Croats and Muslims who joined the army, were these persons dismissed as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there were some Serbs who did not join the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those Serbs who did not join the army, were they dismissed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were dismissed. But I know those who were at home around me in the neighbours. I don't know about the town. But in the company, yes, those who did not join the army, or rather to the reserves, they were all dismissed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were dismissed in 1991; is that correct? It was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there was no war in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who joined the army were sent to Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask some questions regarding the villages. And I will have to mention the names of the villages. And I don't know whether the Prosecutor would prefer us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll go into private session, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Koumjian, I am a little bit lost at this stage, because in a way I have been told the next witness is Rule 92 bis. I've also been told there is a witness in person who is going to give evidence, and I have also been told that there is no statement available. So tell me, Inneke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness is not a protected witness, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, he's not. I was also going to ask Your Honours if I could raise just one very brief matter and perhaps we could take the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could start with the witness after the break. I have a very brief matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We received a communication from the attorney representing -- I'm sure Your Honours and everyone remembers -- the journalist who was summoned. And he has requested a hearing date on that issue of May 10th -- excuse me -- yes, the 10th of May. So if it's possible, that's Mr. Robertson has requested that date for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Strike the name. We had greed not to mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's not the journalist. That's the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the counsel. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel is not protected in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. They never will be. And I know that Ms. Korner had asked me 7th and 9th -- 7th to 9th of May for the witness 7.224. And then she had said 27th to 29th of May for Witness 7.223. So provided there is a common understanding that if we've not -- we are not -- what's the 10th of May? What day is that? Can -- Friday, 10th of May. I'd say -- provisionally I'd say yes, provisionally. But we'd have to reassess or assess the situation at the beginning of that week, that is, on the 3rd or 4th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I remember. Okay. Yes, I suppose -- I suppose we can say yes for the time being, and then we'll see what the situation will be like. Because we would be resuming on the 7th after the Orthodox Easter break, and we will need to take it -- take it up from there. We have a witness coming on the 7th, and he or she is expected to be here until the 9th, which would be fine to introduce the person you've just mentioned on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Fine. I don't think that the witness is planning on being here that date, just counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly, counsel, actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I think he's also requested -- in his letter, he did request be provided with copies of any transcript where the application for the summons was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Koumjian, if we don't have a request from him, if we have a request from you, if you're prepared to make such a request, we will consider it and we will hand down a decision, after -- also after hearing what the Defence have to say, because this is an attorney, an outsider, coming forward and saying, "I want a copy." If I remember well, the transcript would be of a private sitting. I think we went private on that occasion, if I remember well. I'm saying this subject to correction, but I think I'm right. Mr. Ackerman, do you recollect -- do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we started in private session and then decided we could go in public if we didn't mention the names. And then I think I mentioned the name as soon as we went into public and got in trouble for it. That's my recollection. If I'm thinking of the right situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I think most of it is public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are probably right. But in any case, if it's public, I see no problem. I mean, you can -- you can go ahead and hand him a transcript without the need for the Chamber to be aware of that. If it was a private, I think we have to go through a certain procedure. I think we'll break now for half an hour, resuming at 4.45 with this witness, who I understand initially the idea was to tender his statement under Rule 92 bis was not accepted and now he's in person to testify viva voce. 4.45. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Usher, can you bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, first, if I could raise a preliminary matter relating to the last witness. And if I could request to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to be handed a document which contains a solemn declaration to say the truth, the tell the truth. And you are kindly asked to make that solemn declaration loud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, just to make things easy for you, I'll just give you a brief description of where you are. You are in one of the courtrooms of the -- of this Tribunal to give evidence. That's why your presence is required. And we are the three Judges that have been put in charge of this case, and I am the Presiding Judge. To your right, there is the team for the Prosecution. And the lady who is standing will be the one to start putting questions to you. When that is finished, which could be today or Monday- I don't know- you will then be asked questions by the two teams for the Defence. The first team is in the front row to your left, where that gentleman is. And that's the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. Behind, in the back row, there is a lady who is heading at the moment the Defence team for General Talic, not the lady that you have looked at. It's behind the first row, it's the back row. The people -- persons in front of us are officials of the Registry of this Tribunal. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you state your full name.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Fazlagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were born on the 6th of June, 1939 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're known by the nickname Baho?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- in fact, I'm better known as Baho.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your ethnicity is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you practice any religion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're married with two children?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your family moved to Banja Luka in 1952, and you remained there until you left in August of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You attended university and graduated from there in 1962, having studied geography and geology.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And between 1962 and 1974, you worked in the field of education as a teacher and an inspector.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From 1974 until 1981, you were a politician in the municipal government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from 1981, you worked... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whose microphone is not activated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mine, Your Honour -- or not mine. Sorry, I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1991, you worked as chef de cabinet for the municipal government in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No. Up till 1981. From 1973.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In 1981, you then became the director of the Atlas Tourist Agency.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that agency was based in Dubrovnik, but it had a branch office in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, in May of last year, did you give a statement to persons from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that statement was read back to you by an interpreter and you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then in September last year, persons from the Tribunal visited you again and you signed a declaration in relation to that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, were you asked to review your statement again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you asked whether you wanted to clarify anything in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You told me upon reviewing your statement that you wished to change something.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It concerned a date, a formal mistake, a more formal error.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Instead of 1992, it should have been replaced with "1991."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was that in relation to one of the attachments to your statement, attachment number 1?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No. No, not attachment number 1. I believe it was number -- it was either number 11 or 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just give you a copy of your statement in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can just turn to page 2 of the statement, which is also page 2 in the English. In relation to the paragraph numbered 1.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The letter --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. Yes, it should be stated "1991."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also look to paragraph number 13, which is in the -- on page 3 of the English and also the B/C/S. In that paragraph, it states that -- it talks about an interview that you had given a few days after the article listed in point 11. Should that point 11 read "point 12"? So the article that's referred to is the one that's refer to in article 12, directly above that? Sir, are you reading paragraph 13? Paragraph numbered 13 --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it talks about an article listed in point 11. And I think you wanted to tell the Court that you wanted to change that to "point 12, above," which is the paragraph 12 directly above it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where you have "11," it should be "12," in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any other changes that you wished to make in relation to the statement that you have in front of you, in relation to any names?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, except as far as when a military column entered -- I mentioned General Milan Martic, and I didn't mention Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just turn to page 7 of your statement, sir. And it's on page 6 of the English. In the sentence starting "In the spring of 1992, I remember a victory celebration in Banja Luka held for Serb soldiers."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that the paragraph that you're referring to where you mention Ratko Mladic and in fact the person you are referring to is Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Milan Martic, Milan Martic. It refers to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have that folder back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, returning to Atlas. During the time that you were the director, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I was the director of the Atlas branch, Atlas Travel Agency Dubrovnik, the branch in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the time that you were the director, did you not look after all the administrative duties and organise package tours for pleasure and business?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, my branch did. I personally not. But I was -- I gave advice. But I had people who were specialised and who carried on this business.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Atlas agency sold train tickets, airline -- airplane tickets, and bus tickets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: That was a full agency with a full gamut of activities. For bus tickets, airplane ticket, train tickets, sales of package tours, organisation of excursions, organisation of celebrations, if need be, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the company employed 11 staff members at the Banja Luka branch.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you tell what ethnicity these staff members were?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will -- with counsel's permission, can I lead the witness on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not been established when she's asking. I assume that changed, you know, week by week, or month by month. I think the question must be when she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When the company was still the Banja Luka branch of the Dubrovnik office, and there was 11 people -- 11 persons employed, I want to deal with that period of time. And I will take you through the staff members, and you can tell me the ethnicity of those persons. Nada Crljenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: She was -- she's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rada Dobra?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Tijana Crnic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Lukic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Gordana Misiljovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stanka Vukomanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Jozo Kubat?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dragica Vrhovac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Nada Ojdenic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mirsada Gradjanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. In May or June, Atlas formally disbanded because of the war in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No, not in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did Atlas with the office in Dubrovnik formally disband?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It disbanded. And Atlas Prima Tours was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. Between August and the beginning of December, did you take steps to set up a business that was registered in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that company was called Atlas Prima Tours?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you continue to work in the same premises?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were the premises located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: The Veselina Maslese Road, number 1. At the corner of Veselina Maslese and Fra Grga Martic Road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You held the position of director of Atlas Prima Tours until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll go into some more details about your directorship later. I want to ask you some questions now of a more general nature. Were you a member of the Communist Party from 1957 until 1990?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: And before that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you join the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: 1957. I was just a secondary school student.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what year did you join the -- become a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He just said it. 1957 -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question before was: Were you a member of the Communist Party from 1957 until 1990. And the witness answered "And before that as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you attend any political rallies in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when the rally was held that you attended?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the autumn of 1991 probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where was the rally held?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: On the large square in front of the Boska department store. At the time it was called the Edvarda Kardelj square.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in attendance?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: According to my estimate, somewhere between 30 and 40 thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And which party was this rally for?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It was the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall now any of the persons that attended the rally? Sorry --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was Jovan Raskovic; there was Karadzic; Krajisnik; Professor Gugo Lazarevic; Biljana Plavsic; and some more. I can't be sure. There were many more. There were also local ones. But these were the leaders of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know what positions they held at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Raskovic, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: He was the president, I believe, the president of the SDS for the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: The -- he was in the top leadership of the SDS of the Bosnian Serbs. I believe he was the deputy president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Also, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: That is known. President of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Professor Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Then or later he didn't really have an important political position. Professor Lazarevic was, I have to say, a very well known and very well respected Banja Luka intellectual and we all respected him. But at that rally, many of us, we had to change our opinion. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can explain to the Chamber what the general theme of the rally was.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: The general theme was calling for the unity of the Serbian people. And naturally, of course, pointing at what the others were doing, that in fact the moment had come when the Serb people have to be united, and only united could they realise their objective. That was more or less what the topic was, the theme.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did this mean for you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: As for me, personally, this was an exceptionally difficult event. I -- in fact, I could hardly believe that something like this was happening because in Banja Luka we lived in a very multicultural surroundings where we absolutely did not think or even talk about who was who. As far as I'm concerned, I had many more friends who were Serbs than those who were Bosniaks or Croats. And now that we're talking about the Atlas agency that I ran, when you ask me what Nada Crljenica is, as ethnicity, who is even now a citizen, I find it very difficult because even today I cannot make this kind of division to say that Nada is one thing that, Mirsada is another. As long as I live, I will never be able to accept that kind of division. But unfortunately, I am in a position to state these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So how did this rally make you feel?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: At first just like now, I felt very emotional. I couldn't believe that anything was going -- like this was going to happen in a town like this, where we were all one in the same thing. We were all on the promenade, on the beach. What was happening? However, I have to say that clearly what happened is a reflex from that rally that also reflected on the seconds on another side and another on a third side. It is well known that nationalisms will breed new nationalisms. And for us who were unable to accept that -- and there were many of us. I don't only mean -- and I have to say this again. It's not only related to Bosniaks, but also to Croats and to Serbs. Many of us, we were not willing to accept this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, sir, what did you do about this? Did you form a group?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Immediately we reacted. We tried -- those of us who had this opinion, to establish a kind of forum -- intellectuals forum, but of all intellectuals. We called ourselves, as our names were. Boro, Milan, and Ante. But we didn't gather on the grounds of nationality, of ethnicity. But we gathered as a group in the Dom Kultura in the house of culture in the small hall. This is the Dom Kultura, the way we called it, this is Banski Dvor, which is the town hall. And naturally we wanted to have our say, to resist this kind of assault of nationalism -- of nationalisms again, of all kinds. We wanted to resist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want to ask you some questions about weapons. Were you aware of Serbs being armed with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this occur?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: That was already in 1991. That's when it really started going strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you be a little bit more specific in relation to 1991. Was it in the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, already in the beginning of the second half, if not before. But certainly it was in the -- at the beginning of the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where did you see this happening?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Personally -- shall I tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you? Where were you when you saw the Serbs being armed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: One night quite late I came to my mother-in-law's, to my wife's mother, in a location which is in the centre of town. And my mother-in-law called me to the balcony to have a look at something. I went. And just opposite this balcony, there is a sky scraper, perhaps 12 to 15 floors, where -- and we all knew that -- where there were mostly either retired or active military personnel of Serb nationality. I have to say I always find it very hard to specify of Serb ethnicity. And what I saw was a scene which was very obvious. There was a military lorry with military insignia, with soldiers, JNA soldiers. The lorry was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can just stop you there. You said that it was a military lorry with military insignia. What sort of number plates did the vehicle have?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of number plates?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Considering that I was a member of the municipal staff for people's defence for a long time, I know all these insignia and signs, symbols, because I drove these vehicles and I had manoeuvres with these vehicles. They had these typical numbers and letters. There was no doubt that this was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did you see the military personnel doing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, for about an hour they were taking out crates that was of this military colour, olive drab colour. And they were taking these crates into the skyscraper. And I know what was in the crates, because I personally know what is contained in these kind of crates. I know that when I was in the field. And these were weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear who received these weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: As it happens, a lady was an acquaintance of my wife, and in some conversation they happened to have had, said that -- she said that in this skyscraper -- and again I find it difficult to say that the Serbs were getting the weapons from the army, that they were being armed by the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone else inform you about weapons being distributed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. A great friend of mine from a settlement of Borik immediately the following morning he told me when he came to see me -- and he was slightly astonished. He said he came late home and he could hardly get into the skyscraper because there was this military lorry which was parked in reverse next to the skyscraper and that they were carrying crates into the skyscraper. And so we told each other what we thought of this. I told him that the night before, I had watched it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any other occasion that you saw weapons being distributed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: In my apartment where I lived, it was a large building with multi-ethnic citizens who lived there. And one night there was some strange noise. And so we went out to see -- to the window to see what was happening. And what I saw outside parked in front of my entrance --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just tell me when this was, the time.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: April or May -- April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this was in the Starcevica settlement where you lived?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Starcevica that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Sir, can you tell the Court what you saw that evening.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Clearly I was frightened. And through the curtain, I was watching. And I believe that there were five -- but I believe that they were reserves because they always had a little distinguishing feature from active soldiers. The reserves were always a little less tidy. A soldier is a soldier after all. And they were carrying out in front of these five entrances, but only into the apartments where members -- again I find it difficult to say -- of the Serb ethnicity were living. And when this was over, one of them in that area, in that part of that lorry, as far as I could see, he was happy with what he had done. He then fired a burst of gunfire from a machine-gun. And then they just vanished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This lorry that you have described that the soldiers had, was this a military vehicle with, again, JNA insignia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And approximately how long was the lorry parked out the front of your apartment block?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, when did you become aware of the Serbian defence forces, or the SOS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It was beginning of April. I can't tell you the exact date. When I arrived at work, I saw something new for me. It's very close by. In front of the municipality, on the side where Atlas stood, there was a group that I hadn't seen before, a group of soldiers I hadn't seen before. They were very young. I mean, they were young, and they were all well selected. They were all good-looking, and they were all properly dressed, in camouflage uniform of a new kind. And I soon found out that this was a new formation, a new unit, which was called the Serb defence forces, or abbreviation SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. When you said "the municipality," do you mean in front of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. From both corners. From both corners, I could -- I saw them then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I believe there is a problem in interpretation. He did not see -- he did not see the Serb defence forces. The witness said "Serb liberation forces."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. It's a slip of the tongue. I meant defence forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were these -- were these soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: They had some rather modern short-barreled machine-guns. I can't tell you the exact term, because I don't know what these type of weapons are called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you or your family ever harassed by the SOS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: First, when I returned home, my wife who was working in a company in Banja Luka, she was all frightened. And she told me what had happened to her that morning. On the way from Starcevica into town, in the car, she was stopped. She was stopped by the members of presumably this SOS group at the bridge near the student's hostel on the way into town. They ordered her to open the boot. She said that they were quite sharp with her. They checked whether she had weapons. And she was all frightened because this was happening in a free town of Banja Luka. She was disbelieving that this was happening. And at that moment, a lot of things happened to her inwardly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, do you know the accused Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you meet Mr. Brdjanin for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was at the time when he was -- when the president of the municipality was Zivko Radisic and I was his chef de cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what year it was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps at the time just before I left the municipality. But presumably that was in 1980, perhaps 1981. Because we had many meetings with the people who were businessmen in the region. And at the time, Mr. Brdjanin was a businessman. And there were many different meetings that we attended there and in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What business was Mr. Brdjanin in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, Mr. Brdjanin worked in a civil engineering company in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Between 1980 and 1991, how often did you see Mr. Brdjanin after that -- during that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Not often. Not often. Let's say that it was perhaps twice. Maybe more, but I can't recall. Twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have any personal dealings with Mr. Brdjanin in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No, except when there were problems with the Atlas agency. And then my people went to see Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will discuss that in some detail shortly. How often did you see Mr. Brdjanin in Banja Luka during this period?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: In the period when the Crisis Staff of the AP Krajina was established, I saw him very often, as he was going into the building of the municipal assembly in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when did you first become aware of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: As soon as it was established. That was, as far as I can remember -- this was already the end of 1991. And in 1992, they were very active.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would you see Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Regularly, as he went into the municipal assembly building, because they had some premises -- I know where these premises were. I know every part of the municipal building. And so they had these premises there where there was the office of this new body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where were you when you saw Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: My office is in a very interesting position, interesting location. It is between two streets on the corner looking out, between the street of Veselina Maslese and Fra Grga Martic Street, and the Veselina Maslese Street borders the municipal assembly building. So from this corner, I could see everything very well. I could see everything clearly, who was going into the building. Of course, I could see the Banski Dvor, the town hall, and the park.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown this map. And it can be marked Prosecution Exhibit 534 A. Your Honours, copies are being provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait until we get our copy so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I just asked counsel to wait until we get our copies. Yes. Are we going to put the map on the ELMO so that -- if the witness is going to be asked to identify or point to places, I think that's the way to go about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, he will, sir. I just want to give him a chance to orient himself with the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, is this a portion of a -- a larger map that you saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And have you got your bearings on the map?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please place it on this machine to your right. Sir, if you can just put the -- give it to the usher. Can you take a pen that's by the side of the machine. Not black. Any colour but black. Not black. And can you just point, first of all without marking it -- but can you just point to where your office is located -- was located, Atlas. And if you can do it on the ELMO machine, not on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: What I'm showing is the street of Veselina Maslese.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can point it out on the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, fine. [In English] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That marking the document, if you can just point to the place where Atlas Prima Tours offices were.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Here. Here. Exactly here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can mark that with the letter "A," where the offices are. If you can mark that with the letter "A."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to mark it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where the offices were.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could you put your initials next to that "A," please, your initials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can now point without marking, but just point to where the municipal building is on that map.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where the municipal building is, can you mark that with the letter "M," please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I'll do it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also initial it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness can now be given this diagram. Do you have that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a diagram. But it doesn't have a -- an exhibit number as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that can be Prosecution Exhibit P535.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about the numbers, sir. Let us worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Copies of this diagram have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a diagram which is dated 11/4/2002; no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell the Court what this is a diagram of.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: It represents an amateur diagram of the location of Atlas, of the municipality building, the park in which the orthodox church is now being built, and the Banski Dvor, the Hotel Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if you'd just like to place that on the ELMO next to you. If you can just point to where your offices were located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you point to the municipal building, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is the building directly in front of that building? Sorry. Sorry. For the record, you're pointing to the building marked "Skupstina opstina."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the building directly in front of that is what?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: This?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: We called it the house of culture. But it's been also known as the Palace of the Ban, Banski Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And you're pointing now to Banski Dvor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The building to the left of that, marked "SDK," what was in that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Here money was deposited after the daily transactions. It was also here that we carried the money at the end of the day, the money that we collected by the sales of tickets, all the transactions were carried here -- were registered here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the financial accounting building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the Atlas building. Whereabouts was your office within that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Right at the very corner on the floor, with a small protruding balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just mark -- can you just take one of those pens again and mark where the balcony protruded out from the corner of the building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you initialise it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And so from -- it was this position on the balcony, the window balcony, that you were able to see Mr. Brdjanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So how far from the balcony window to the entrance of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: From 7 to 10 metres. That's my assessment. And as far as I believe my eyesight is good. From 7 to 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with those -- the diagram. That can be returned to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment. Before the diagram is returned, there is a signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, whose signature is that on the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And were you asked to sign and date it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, from that balcony in the Atlas office, can you tell the Court the names of any people you saw entering the municipal building during the time period that you were referring to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that I didn't know exactly who were all the members of the Crisis Staff, I will tell you the names for whom then I learned later were members of the staff. Milan Puvacic, my good friend; then Dr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did you -- I'm sorry. How often did you see Mr. Puvacic enter the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I've known him from my secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know his occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was -- he had a legal background. And he was a judge and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who else did you see?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how long have you known Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the visits to the municipal bodies and visits to the hospital, I did see him. I met him. I already -- from 1985 or 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how often would you see him enter the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, practically every morning. Before entering the building, he would buy at the kiosk, which was right across the road, he would be buying the newspapers, cigarettes. And with the newspaper and cigarettes, he would enter the municipal building in uniform. And with a very market -- very big pistol on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was this the kiosk that you drew that is across from the office in the drawing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone else entering the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the president -- namely, the mayor would enter every morning. But of course, there's no question whether he attended or not the Crisis Staff. But you see, he -- that was his headquarters. Then there was Rajko Kasagic, then Dr. Milanovic, then some --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we can just go back to Mr. Radic. How long had you known Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, at least some 20 and more years, because Mr. Predrag Radic played in the team -- football team Borac and I was also active on that team. So on that basis, we knew each other quite well. And we were also pleased when at that occasion, Mr. Radic was appointed to the head of the municipality in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Had you known Mr. Radic for some 25 years at that point?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Exhibit P227, which is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, issue number 2 of 92.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that document, sir, can you tell us how long had you known Mr. Kasagic for.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I've heard about him. At the time he still wasn't in Banja Luka. And then when he did come, then I saw him, let's say, rather frequently, quite frequently, particularly in town; then at other events; and also I paid him once a personal visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how often did you see him enter the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Every morning, except when he was on a business trip, because he had -- he was occupying a certain position. That was de facto the Banja Luka government. It was -- it's -- it was termed as the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could look at the second decision that's published in that Official Gazette. If you can turn to the second page of that document. That is a decision of the 5th of May, 1992 listing members of the ARK Crisis Staff. If we can go down that list of persons, can you tell me which of those persons you saw enter the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've told us about Mr. Brdjanin. You said that you saw him quite often entering the building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did you see Vojo Kupresanin enter the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't observe this every morning. I had also other matters to attend to. But I did see him at least a few times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how long had you known Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately as long as Mr. Brdjanin, because Mr. Vojo was -- came when the president -- Zivko Radisic was the president, and he was co-opted in one of the bodies, at the regional level, of course prior to these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Predrag Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Radislav Vukic, Dr. Milan Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long have you known Dr. Milanovic for?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Very long indeed. Since the time when -- Mr. Seid Maglajlija was the mayor of Banja Luka. We were contacting quite frequently in connection with the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what year you first met Dr. Milanovic approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how often did you see him entering the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I've mentioned -- I stated before that I wasn't standing there intentionally every morning, like Inspector Maigret [phoen] but occasionally I would stand up and look, maybe three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you continue.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long have you known Stojan Zupljanin for?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known him a rather long time. He worked in the Secretariat of Interior. Now it's called the Ministry of Interior, the police. And he was close to a group of persons, to which I was also close. So we did see each other and have a drink together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did he enter the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Often. When I looked, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General Momir Talic, did you ever see him enter the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how did you know General Talic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, General Talic was an impressive figure of a general, and he would stand out. And it was easy to notice him, and it was a face one would remember. And I know the gentleman not personally, but I attended secondary school in Banja Luka together with his brother, if that is his brother. But I believe that was -- that is his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many times did you see General Talic enter the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
