utterances.text: Well, I don't think more than twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is there anybody else on that list that you have in front of you that you saw enter the building? You have mentioned Mr. Puvacic already.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Puvacic very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides him, is there anybody else on the remainder of the list?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Djuro Bulic, who also worked in the police. I think he was the deputy chief. They often changed. I saw him quite frequently. The others, I can't remember them by their names, but I probably knew these people. But quite some time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that exhibit can be returned to the registry, and if the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit 181. I've provided the Defence and also the registry today with both pages of that exhibit with better copies of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, do you have a single sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but it's -- there's material on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment. Witness, if you can just look at the front page of that newspaper. It's the Glas newspaper dated the 9th of May, 1992. What is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: This is from -- a picture from one of the regional centres premises of information dissemination in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where is that room located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: In the cellar of the municipal building. And closed off with reinforced steel doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: When it was inaugurated, the celebration for its inauguration. And I wouldn't know the exact year. Seid Maglajlija was still the municipal president. It must have been somewhere in 1970s. End of the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this the only room to the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: No. Inside in it, there were two or three other rooms with printers, fax machines, Telex machines. And for those -- at those times, it was considered to be the most modern such facility in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was this centre used to disseminate and receive information from Banja Luka and other municipalities and republic authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was of a wider importance. As for Banja Luka, those of us who lived there, we all know that Banja Luka covered, in fact, a wider area. And that's -- normally it was a regional centre. Because all this information that was gathered was collected there. Information that was gathered was sent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you to turn to the other page, page 3 of the article. Do you recognise any one of the persons sitting at that table?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Three of them very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From left -- going from left to right, can you name them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Miro Mladenovic. He was the editor-in-chief of the Glas newspaper. Then Mr. Milanovic. The second man, I don't know. The second man, I don't know. I mean, the photograph doesn't really tell me anything. So the third man is Dr. Milanovic. And this next man I still don't know. It's a very recognisable face that I know, but I can't remember. And then Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see Radoslav Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. He must be looking at a different photograph than we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are looking at this one, Mr. Ackerman, on the -- what Ms. Sutherland said, the third page -- well, actually it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhibit 181.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He has five people there, and I only see four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Five -- he has five people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only see four people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are five people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three, four, five.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you've got the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would explain it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not looking at the same photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not. Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, could you please give this to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It makes a great deal of sense now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really watch television all that much. Very often we had electricity cuts in our locality. But let's say that I may have seen him twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when was it that you saw him on television? During what period of time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: That would be in that period when the Crisis Staff was active, which would have been 1992, 1992 spring, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the general nature of his speeches?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as we are concerned, those of us who couldn't really face this time, this period of time, it was difficult. It was hard. It was unacceptable. It was a general call to something that we couldn't accept. And we couldn't understand that anybody could be speaking like this. About, for instance, Mr. Brdjanin was giving some data about Bosniaks in that area, saying that only a certain number of Bosniaks would stay in that area. There were some figures that were being given, some 2.000, and there were some percentages being talked about, a certain percentage. And what that meant, 5 to 6 per cent, which means that 95 per cent would have to leave their native land, among whom, of course, I was forced to do the same, unfortunately. I had to leave my town, a town that I had given everything to. And I'm wondering why, why I left. What did I actually do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall reading any articles or newspapers written by Mr. Brdjanin -- about Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: These were mostly reports about the work and the decisions of the Crisis Staff, where the public was given some announcements about actions undertaken against the Serbs. And such an article would in fact make me cry as well as laugh. It would upset me, make me emotional, and I would be also disbelieving of this. And I could quote Mr. Brdjanin's words to you, that I, Ibrahim Fazlagic, was a drastic case, a radical case, because out of the six dismissed members of personnel, I had dismissed six members who were Serbs, of Serb ethnicity, which wasn't true, and that this was unacceptable and it could just not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will deal with that issue in a moment. Just getting back to the newspaper articles that talked about things that Mr. Brdjanin had said, was there anything else that you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, later I read some decisions. As I said, this is mostly related to decisions in the newspapers. We would just read decisions about the general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin on the radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't listen to the radio often, but I think I heard him at least once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which time -- what time period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the same period in 1992, this period when there were these upheavals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what he said on the radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the details. But the theme, general theme, was what I had heard on TV about the activities that have to be undertaken. What he presented really was a kind of platform, a programme about what was to follow, what had to be done. And these activities really ended up happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 137. And this is a Glas newspaper dated the 9th of -- 4th of April. I'm sorry. Your Honour, I provided both the registrar and the Defence with better copies of the photograph that's contained within that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, how many people appear in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I can see four.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the persons in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: All four of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So from left to right, can you please tell the Court who they are.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC
utterances.text: I think this is Stojan Zupljanin, Predrag Radic, Mr. Brdjanin, and Mr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time, and I think this would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Sir, we are going to stop here for today. We will continue again on Monday in the afternoon, like today. You will come here at -- we will start the -- continue hearing your evidence at 2.15 on Monday. But you will be advised at what time -- exactly what time you are required to be here. The witness can be escorted out. In the meantime, between now and next Monday, please, you are not allowed to speak to anyone or contact -- have any contact with anyone with regard to this case or with regard to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that brings us to the end of our labours for this week. I wish you all a nice weekend, and we'll meet again on Monday at 2.15. Thank you.
